name: ECG 3 · Rhythms
blurb: Name every common fast, slow and irregular rhythm on a strip.

topics.name: Why arrhythmias happen
topics.desc: What an arrhythmia is, how it starts, and how we catch it.

cards.q: A single early beat in an otherwise normal strip is
cards.a:
An arrhythmia: a disturbance of the site of origin

Any disturbance of rate, regularity, origin or conduction counts, even one aberrant beat.

cards.q:
A resting rate of 38 in a fit marathon runner is necessarily pathological.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Rates as low as 35–40 are common and normal in well-trained athletes.

cards.q: Syncope during an arrhythmia is mainly due to
cards.a:
Fall in cardiac output

Light-headedness and syncope are symptoms of decreased cardiac output.

cards.q: Enhanced automaticity is a disorder of
cards.a:
Impulse formation

A non-sinus site generates new impulses fast enough to overdrive the sinus node.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.134; Khan ch1 p.4

cards.q: What sets up a re-entry circuit?
cards.a:
Two pathways that conduct at different speeds

A slow pathway lets the impulse return and loop: a disorder of impulse transmission.

cards.q:
A premature beat can be the trigger that starts a sustained tachycardia.
True or false?
cards.a: True. AVNRT usually starts with a premature beat; a PVC on the T wave can start VT.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.144, 158, 163; Khan ch11 p.249

cards.q: Match each letter of HIS DEBS
cards.a:
H: Hypoxia
S: Sympathetic stimulation
E: Electrolytes
B: Bradycardia

HIS DEBS lists the arrhythmogenic factors to check in every patient.

cards.q: Why run a rhythm strip when an arrhythmia is suspected?
cards.a:
It shows many more beats, catching intermittent events

A long tracing captures irregularities and bursts missed by the few beats of a 12-lead.

cards.q: Syncope occurs a few times a year. Which device is most likely to capture it?
cards.a:
Implanted event recorder

An implanted recorder stays in for over a year and records automatically.

cards.q: Match each type to its mechanism
cards.a:
Sinus origin: Normal pathway, wrong rate or regularity
Ectopic: Focus outside the sinus node
Re-entrant: Impulse trapped in a circuit
Pre-excitation: Accessory pathway shortcut

These four plus conduction blocks make Thaler's five basic types.

topics.name: Sinus rhythms
topics.desc: Fast, slow, irregular and silent sinus nodes, and who rescues them.

cards.q: Explain: Sinus tachycardia: sinus beats over 100
cards.a: Every QRS has a normal sinus P wave in front, but the rate is over 100. This is sinus tachycardia. Strenuous exercise drives it normally.

cards.q: An 80-year-old has unexplained sinus tachycardia and nothing else. Which cause does Thaler flag?
cards.a:
Hyperthyroidism

Sinus tachycardia can be the only presenting sign of hyperthyroidism in the elderly.

cards.q: Explain: Sinus bradycardia: sinus beats under 60
cards.a: Normal sinus P waves before every QRS, but the rate is below 60: sinus bradycardia. It is typical in well-conditioned athletes at rest.

cards.q: Which drug class most commonly causes sinus bradycardia?
cards.a:
Beta-blockers

Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and opioids are the commonest drug causes.

cards.q:
In sinus arrhythmia, the heart rate rises during inspiration.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Inspiration accelerates the sinus rate and expiration slows it.

cards.q: A perfectly fixed RR interval in a 60-year-old with long-standing diabetes suggests
cards.a:
Autonomic neuropathy

Loss of sinus arrhythmia reflects diminished autonomic feedback, typical of diabetic neuropathy.

cards.q: During a sinus arrest the strip shows
cards.a:
No P waves and no QRS complexes

The sinus node is silent, so neither atria nor ventricles are activated.

cards.q:
A pause exactly twice the normal cycle length favours sinus exit block over sinus arrest.
True or false?
cards.a: True. In exit block the node kept firing silently, so it resumes on its usual beat.

cards.q: Match each pacemaker to its intrinsic rate
cards.a:
Sinus node: 60–100
Atrial: 60–75
Junctional: 40–60
Ventricular: 30–45

The lower the pacemaker, the slower its intrinsic rate.

cards.q: An 80-year-old faints. Monitor: fast AF stops, a 5-second pause, then slow sinus beats. Diagnosis?
cards.a:
Sick sinus syndrome

Tachycardia alternating with bradycardia and a long post-termination pause is the tachy-brady syndrome.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.178; Khan ch11 p.283

topics.name: Premature beats
topics.desc: Early atrial and ventricular beats, their patterns and when they matter.

cards.q: Explain: A PAC comes early with a different P
cards.a: A premature atrial complex (PAC) arises in the atrium away from the sinus node. Its P wave comes too early and has a different shape. The QRS is usually narrow and normal.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.140–141; Khan ch11 p.249

cards.q: The cycle after a PAC is typically
cards.a:
Less than compensatory

The PAC resets the sinus node, so the next sinus beat comes sooner than a full compensatory pause.

cards.q: A pause follows a T wave that looks peaked compared with the others. Most likely cause?
cards.a:
A blocked PAC hidden in the T wave

Non-conducted PACs are the commonest cause of pauses; the P deforms the preceding T.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.143; Khan ch11 p.249

cards.q: Explain: A PVC is early, wide and bizarre
cards.a: A premature ventricular complex (PVC) starts in the ventricle and spreads slowly through muscle. It is early, wide (at least 0.12 s in most leads) and bizarre, with no P wave before it and an ST–T pointing opposite to the QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.157; Khan ch11 p.253

cards.q:
A fully compensatory pause after an early beat favours a PVC over a PAC.
True or false?
cards.a: True. The sinus node keeps its timing after a PVC, so the pause is fully compensatory.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.157; Khan ch11 p.253

cards.q: Explain: Bigeminy and trigeminy are fixed patterns
cards.a: When PVCs alternate with sinus beats one to one, it is bigeminy. Two sinus beats then one PVC is trigeminy. PACs can do the same: atrial bigeminy.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.157; Khan ch11 p.249, 254

cards.q: Two consecutive PVCs are called
cards.a:
A couplet

A run of two PVCs is a couplet; bigeminy means alternating with sinus beats.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.159; Khan ch11 p.253

cards.q:
PVCs that vary in shape and coupling interval are unifocal.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Varying shape and coupling means several foci: multifocal, or multiform.
cards.note: Khan ch11 p.253, 257; Thaler ch3 p.158

cards.q: Why is an R-on-T PVC dangerous?
cards.a:
It falls in the vulnerable period and can trigger VT

The T wave is the vulnerable period; a PVC there can start VT or VF.

cards.q: Which PVC is most worrying?
cards.a:
A PVC during an acute myocardial infarction

Any PVC in acute MI can trigger VT or VF: one of the rules of malignancy.

topics.name: Narrow-complex tachycardias
topics.desc: SVT, fibrillation, flutter, MAT and atrial tachycardia, told apart.

cards.q: Explain: AVNRT: sudden, regular, 150 to 250
cards.a: AVNRT (AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, often just "SVT") is an absolutely regular narrow tachycardia at 150–250. It starts and stops abruptly, often in a normal heart. A rate above 230 should prompt a search for WPW (level 4).
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.144; Khan ch11 p.265

cards.q: Explain: In AVNRT the P is hidden
cards.a: Atria and ventricles fire almost together, so in over half of cases the P wave is buried in the QRS. Otherwise a retrograde P distorts the end of the QRS: a pseudo-S in II, III, aVF or a pseudo-r′ in V1.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.144; Khan ch11 p.265–267

cards.q: Explain: AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves
cards.a: In atrial fibrillation many tiny re-entrant circuits make atrial activity chaotic. There are no P waves, only a flat or undulating fibrillatory baseline, and the QRS complexes come irregularly irregularly.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.149; Khan ch11 p.281

cards.q: AF at a ventricular rate of 160 is described as AF with
cards.a:
Rapid ventricular response

A fast ventricular rate in AF is a rapid ventricular response.

cards.q: Explain: Flutter: a sawtooth at about 300
cards.a: In atrial flutter one re-entrant circuit around the tricuspid valve drives the atria at 250–350, often 300. There is no flat baseline: flutter (F) waves form a sawtooth, best seen in II, III and aVF, with spiky P-like waves in V1.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.147; Khan ch11 p.277–279

cards.q: Atrial flutter at 300 per minute with 4:1 block. What is the ventricular rate?
cards.a:
75 bpm

One in four F waves conducts: 300 ÷ 4 = 75.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.147; Khan ch11 p.279

cards.q: Explain: Sawtooth versus chaos
cards.a: Flutter is organised: identical F waves at a fixed rate, and a regular QRS if the block is fixed. AF is chaos: no repeating atrial wave and an irregularly irregular QRS. Flutter with variable block is irregular but not truly chaotic.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.150; Khan ch11 p.281

cards.q: Explain: MAT: three P shapes, irregular
cards.a: Multifocal atrial tachycardia comes from several atrial foci firing at random. It is irregular, rate 100–200, but unlike AF each QRS has a P wave. You need at least three P-wave shapes. It is common in severe lung disease such as COPD.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.153; Khan ch11 p.270–271

cards.q: A patient on digoxin shows a regular atrial rhythm at 180 with 2:1 conduction and a flat baseline between P waves. Most likely?
cards.a:
Paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with block

Digitalis excess classically gives atrial tachycardia with AV block; the baseline between P waves is isoelectric.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.154; Khan ch11 p.268–269

cards.q: Match each rhythm to its response to adenosine or carotid massage
cards.a:
AVNRT: Terminates
Atrial flutter: Slows, revealing F waves
Atrial tachycardia: More AV block
MAT: No effect

Only rhythms using the AV node in their circuit stop; the rest are just unmasked.

topics.name: Wide-complex tachycardias
topics.desc: VT, torsades, VF, AIVR, and telling VT from aberrant SVT.

cards.q: Explain: VT: three or more PVCs in a row
cards.a: A run of three or more consecutive PVCs is ventricular tachycardia, usually at 120–200. When every complex looks alike it is monomorphic; that form is typical of a scar from a healed infarct.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.159–160; Khan ch11 p.253

cards.q:
A 6-beat run of VT that stops on its own is sustained VT.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Sustained means over 30 seconds or haemodynamically unstable; a self-terminating 6-beat run is non-sustained.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.159; Khan ch11 p.254

cards.q: Explain: Torsades: VT that twists
cards.a: Torsade de pointes is a polymorphic VT: the QRS spirals around the baseline, swinging in amplitude and axis, at 200–300. It usually arises on a prolonged QT, often started by a PVC on the long T wave, and can degenerate into VF.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.162–163; Khan ch11 p.293

cards.q: Explain: VF: no QRS, no output
cards.a: In ventricular fibrillation the tracing jerks about (coarse) or undulates gently (fine) with no true QRS complexes. The heart pumps nothing. It is the commonest rhythm in adult sudden death: start CPR and defibrillate at once.

cards.q: Wide regular complexes at 75 just after a blocked coronary artery is opened. Best action?
cards.a:
Observe: likely accelerated idioventricular rhythm

AIVR at 50–100 after reperfusion is benign and rarely needs treatment.

cards.q:
A wide-complex tachycardia can be supraventricular in origin.
True or false?
cards.a: True. Aberrant conduction through a refractory bundle branch widens a supraventricular beat.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.164–165; Khan ch11 p.286

cards.q: A 68-year-old with an old anterior MI has a regular wide tachycardia at 180 and is alert. Working diagnosis?
cards.a:
Ventricular tachycardia

Prior MI favours VT, and a wide regular tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise, even when stable.
cards.note: Khan ch11 p.286; Thaler ch3 p.167

cards.q: Explain: Capture beats prove AV dissociation
cards.a: In VT the atria often keep their own sinus rhythm: AV dissociation, with P waves marching through independently. It is seen in fewer than 45%. Now and then a P slips through and gives one narrow, normal QRS: a capture beat.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.167–168; Khan ch11 p.287, 290–291

cards.q: Explain: Fusion beats are half and half
cards.a: If a sinus impulse arrives while the ventricular focus is also firing, the two depolarise the ventricles together. The fusion beat looks part normal, part VT. It is seen in only about 15% of VT but strongly supports it.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.168; Khan ch11 p.287

cards.q: Explain: Read V1 to V6 for VT
cards.a: Khan's precordial clues for VT: - all QRS negative in V1–V6 (negative concordance): diagnostic - a QR complex in any of V2–V6, or R to S nadir over 0.1 s - QRS over 0.14 s, or axis −90° to ±180°

topics.name: Slow rhythms and escape
topics.desc: Junctional and ventricular escape, asystole, and when to pace.

cards.q: A narrow beat without a P wave appears after a 2-second pause. It is
cards.a:
A junctional escape beat

It came late, after a pause, so it is an escape beat.

cards.q: Explain: Junctional escape: narrow, 40 to 60
cards.a: When the sinus node fails, the AV junction usually takes over. A junctional escape rhythm is regular, 40–60, with a narrow QRS because the ventricles are still activated through the normal pathways. There is no normal P wave.

cards.q: Explain: The retrograde P points backwards
cards.a: Often no P wave is seen. If atria are activated backwards from the junction, a retrograde P appears: inverted in II, upright in aVR. It may sit before (PR under 0.11 s), inside or after the QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.132; Khan ch11 p.252

cards.q: A regular narrow rhythm at 85 with no P waves in a patient on digoxin. Most likely?
cards.a:
Accelerated junctional rhythm

Faster than the 40–60 escape rate, narrow and P-less: an accelerated junctional rhythm, a digoxin toxicity sign.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.134; ch4 p.192; Khan ch10 p.232–233

cards.q: Wide QRS complexes, no P waves, regular at 35. The rhythm is
cards.a:
Ventricular escape (idioventricular)

Wide, P-less and in the 30–45 range: a ventricular escape focus.

cards.q:
Slow wide escape beats should be suppressed with an antiarrhythmic like PVCs.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Escape beats are a rescue; suppressing them could leave no rhythm at all.

cards.q: Explain: Asystole: no ventricular activity
cards.a: Asystole is prolonged electrical inactivity: a flat line with no QRS. Sometimes P waves continue alone (P-wave asystole). Confirm it in more than one lead, since fine VF can look flat.

cards.q: Very slow, wide, shapeless complexes in a patient without a pulse are best called
cards.a:
Agonal rhythm

Slow, wide, deteriorating complexes in a failing heart form an agonal rhythm.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.130–131 (escape, asystole); term not used in either book

cards.q: A man with tachy-brady syndrome faints during 5-second pauses. Definitive treatment?
cards.a:
Permanent pacemaker

Symptomatic sick sinus syndrome is a leading indication for a pacemaker.
